ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Leveraging Bidirectional Transformers for De Novo Peptide Sequencing
PROPOSAL: Experiment to evaluate the effect of incorporating bidirectional self-attention into the Transformer-based architecture used in the recent state-of-the-art de novo peptide sequencing model, SwinER-Transformer.
CONTROLS: Compare two versions of SwinER-Transformer: one using unidirectional self-attention and the other using bidirectional self-attention, using the same hyperparameters and training setup.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (splitting the computation between training and evaluation)
PREDICTION: The bidirectional Transformer should improve the accuracy of peptide sequencing on real-world MS/MS datasets, potentially rivaling state-of-the-art performance, but it may require more computational resources to train.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Embedding of Bidirectional Context for Autoregressive Peptide Sequence Generation
PROPOSAL: Experiment to design and evaluate an efficient embedding mechanism for incorporating bidirectional context into the autoregressive peptide sequence generator architecture, replacing the need for expensive auxiliary length predictors found in non-autoregressive models.
CONTROLS: Compare the proposed embedding mechanism to the standard Model-based sequence prediction technique (MSP) and an MLP baselines on SwinER-Transformer without bidirectional self-attention (for unidirectional comparison).
COST: 50 GPU-hours (efficient implementation should be prioritized)
PREDICTION: The proposed embedding mechanism should enable SwinER-Transformer to leverage bidirectional context more efficiently, improving both accuracy and computational efficiency, potentially leading to a new state-of-the-art in de novo peptide sequencing.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Pre-Trained Language Models for Zero-Shot Generalization in De Novo Peptide Sequencing
PROPOSAL: Experiment to explore whether pre-trained language models (e.g., BERT, RoBERTa) can be fine-tuned for zero-shot generalization in de novo peptide sequencing, using real-world datasets from different sources (e.g., antibody sequencing, post-translational modification identification).
CONTROLS: Compare fine-tuned pre-trained language models to a SwinER-Transformer model that is trained only on the dataset of interest, using metrics such as peptide sequence accuracy and cross-modality generalization.
COST: 150 GPU-hours (leveraging large pre-trained language models)
PREDICTION: Pre-trained language models should generalize well to unseen datasets and potentially adapt quickly to new sequence domains, improving the zero-shot performance but might not reach state-of-art in any particular setting due to the specifics of the domain.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Evaluating Pre-Trained Language Models for Zero-Shot Generalization in De Novo Peptide Sequencing
PROPOSAL: REVISED: Experiment to explore whether a Transformer-based approach that incorporates pre-trained language model weights (e.g., BERT, RoBERTa) into the SwinER-Transformer architecture can improve zero-shot generalization in de novo peptide sequencing, using real-world datasets from different sources (e.g., antibody sequencing, post-translational modification identification).
CONTROLS: Compare the revised Transformer-based model with SwinER-Transformer that is trained only on the dataset of interest, with and without fine-tuning pre-trained language models, using metrics such as peptide sequence accuracy and cross-modality generalization.
COST: No additional GPU-hours (leveraging pre-trained weights)
PREDICTION: Incorporating pre-trained language models into the SwinER-Transformer should improve zero-shot generalization by adapting to unseen datasets and sequence domains, potentially rivaling state-of-art performance but with more reliable training and less sensitivity to hyperparameters.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Bidirectional Context Insertion for Error Correction in De Novo Peptide Sequencing
PROPOSAL: Experiment to explore whether incorporating bidirectional context into a standard autoregressive peptide sequence generator can improve error correction for de novo peptide sequencing, using a simple scheme to inject bidirectional context at erroneous positions.
CONTROLS: Compare the proposed bidirectional context insertion scheme to a standard autoregressive sequence generator with and without a separate error correction phase, using metrics such as peptide sequence accuracy and edit distance improvement.
COST: 80 GPU-hours (implementation should be efficient)
PREDICTION: The proposed bidirectional context insertion scheme should improve error correction in de novo peptide sequencing by leveraging long-range dependencies in the sequence, potentially leading to more accurate sequence inference.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Scaffolded Training for Stabilizing Bidirectional Modeling in De Novo Peptide Sequencing
PROPOSAL: Experiment to evaluate the impact of a scaffolded training scheme, which involves pre-training a unidirectional model on synthetic peptide sequences and then fine-tuning the pre-trained model on real-world datasets to stabilize bidirectional modeling in de novo peptide sequencing.
CONTROLS: Compare the proposed scaffolded training scheme to standard fine-tuning of a pre-trained bidirectional model and a directly trained autoregressive model, using metrics such as peptide sequence accuracy and convergence speed.
COST: 120 GPU-hours (longer training times for pre-training and fine-tuning)
PREDICTION: Scaffolded training should stabilize bidirectional modeling and reduce the challenges associated with optimizing complex objectives, leading to more accurate and robust sequence inference.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing the Impact of Tokenization Schemes on Bidirectional Modeling in De Novo Peptide Sequencing
PROPOSAL: Experiment to investigate how different tokenization schemes (e.g., subword modeling, character-level modeling) affect the performance of bidirectional models in de novo peptide sequencing, using the scaffolded training scheme as a baseline.
CONTROLS: Compare the impact of different tokenization schemes on peptide sequence accuracy and convergence speed, using standard autoregressive and bidirectional models with and without scaffolded training.
COST: 60 GPU-hours (tokenization schemes require minor adaptation of the models)
PREDICTION: The choice of tokenization scheme should have a noticeable impact on bidirectional modeling in de novo peptide sequencing, with some schemes providing better performance on specific types of sequences (e.g., short peptides vs. long peptides).

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Domain-Adversarial Training for Improving Generalization in De Novo Peptide Sequencing
PROPOSAL: Experiment to evaluate the impact of domain-adversarial training on the performance of bidirectional models in de novo peptide sequencing, using pseudo-labels from a separate domain as adversarial examples.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of domain-adversarial training to standard training and scaffolded training, using metrics such as peptide sequence accuracy and convergence speed, on real-world datasets from different sources (e.g., antibody sequencing, post-translational modification identification).
COST: 180 GPU-hours (generating pseudo-labels requires additional computation)
PREDICTION: Domain-adversarial training should improve the generalization of bidirectional models in de novo peptide sequencing by reducing overfitting to specific domains and improving robustness to distribution shifts.

ACTION: ADD

PROPOSAL: Experiment to design and evaluate hierarchical architectures that integrate multiple levels of representation, from residue-wise to smaller peptide segments, for efficient bidirectional modeling in de novo peptide sequencing.
CONTROLS: Compare the proposed hierarchical architectures to standard autoregressive and bidirectional models, using metrics such as peptide sequence accuracy and computational efficiency, on a variety of real-world datasets from different sources (e.g., antibody sequencing, post-translational modification identification).
COST: 200 GPU-hours (larger models require significant additional computation)
PREDICTION: Hierarchical architectures should improve the efficiency and accuracy of bidirectional modeling in de novo peptide sequencing by better capturing complex relationships between residues and sequence segments, potentially leading to a new state-of-art in this domain.

PREDICTION: The chosen method should handle variable-length sequences effectively and accurately, allowing for better application and analysis of de novo peptide sequencing in proteomics and other protein science fields.

TITLE: Augmenting Autoregressive Generators with Bidirectional Prophet Net
PROPOSAL: Compare popular autoregressive (AR) models (e.g. BART, T5, SSR) with an augmented version incorporating a bidirectional Prophet Net module [1], designed to capture global contextual relationships between distant sequence positions. The Prophet Net module uses a combination of recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and a MLP to predict the next sequence token after attending to all input tokens simultaneously. We expect this integration to significantly improve sequence quality and capture biological structure in de novo peptide sequencing tasks, where context globally complicates peptides.
CONTROLS: Compare against standard AR models and explore key design decisions, such as gross architecture choice and the inclusion of domain-specific biolographic knowledge.
COST: 16,000 GPU hours.
PREDICTION: The augmented model should show improved scores on benchmark datasets in de novo peptide sequencing compared to autoregressive baselines, and offer both qualitative and quantitative interpretations of the bidirectional learning mechanism's effectiveness.

[1] This module is a graph-based node attentions mechanism from the Prophet Attention paper - we will slightly adapt this to coherentently build bidirectional connections about sequence elements.

CTC loss can help reduce the "vanishing gradient" problem associated with training autoregressive models to predict entire sequences at once.
CONTROLS: Compare performance with other objectives (e.g. sequence-level token-wise objective, uniform perplexity metric) and analyze the impact of sequence length and bidirectional attentions.
COST: 12,000 GPU hours.
PREDICTION: We expect the use of CTC loss to result in models that better capture bidirectional dependencies and reduce sequence reconstruction errors, while also maintaining the advantages of AR models in terms of tractable, efficient sequential modeling.

title: bidirectional autoregressive model for de novo peptide sequencing
PROPOSAL: Develop a variant of the Transformer-XL architecture that can model bidirectional context while maintaining autoregressive generation. This will be achieved by incorporating a backward attention mechanism that considers both forward and backward context when predicting each token. To stabilize training, a "cache" mechanism will be introduced that accumulates the output of the forward attention and provides it to the backward attention step after a specified number of iterations. This willalso help in avoiding the vanishing gradients problem seen in traditional autoregressive models.
CONTROLS: A standard Transformer-XL model (base line for AR), a standard Transformer-XL model with backtracking bidirectional self-attention (extends the work on use bidirectional self-attention of NAR to AR) and a standard Transformer-XL model with a strong noise objective added to prevent overfitting in long sequences (evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of bidirectional AR and unidirectional AR with increased assumed knowledge of sequence)
COST: 500
PREDICTION: Improved generation accuracy for longer sequences (> 20 amino acids) and signal peptide short length (lower 5% of amino acid sequence lengths), with marginal decrease in speed (≤ 10%). A narrower delta is expected when the function gap between the range of our bidirectional perspective versus bidirectional NAR is compared with our base case. The model may struggle with repetitive sequences because of the aforementioned disruption of the cache mechanism.

TITLE:  architecture comparison: bert, transformer-xl, and lux model for de novo peptide sequencing
PROPOSAL: Investigate the benefits of different architectures for de novo peptide sequencing by comparing the performance of BERT, Transformer-XL, and LXU models on the same benchmark dataset. To address the real-world variability in sequence lengths, an ablation study is conducted to evaluate the impact of sequence length on model performance for each architecture. This will help identify which architectures are best suiting de novo peptide sequencing tasks depending on the sequence length and other parameters.
CONTROLS: The three models are the exact implementations used by the paper "ALBERT: A Lite BERT for Self-Supervised Learning of Language Representations" for BERT, "Transformer-XL: Attentive Interpretable Model for Long Context" for Transformer-XL and "LXU: An Extreme Long-Range Contextualised Representation Model" for LXU. Training details, models are built based on their standard methods described for use in protein sequence prediction
